impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that grants an exclusive license but retains the right to sue third parties for infringement retains sufficient exclusionary rights to establish constitutional standing to bring an infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner who licenses certain rights exclusively but retains the right to sue for infringement possesses a non-illusory exclusionary right sufficient to satisfy Article III standing. The decision clarifies the boundaries of patent standing when rights are split between licensors and licensees.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners structuring license agreements can retain standing to enforce patents against third-party infringers even after granting exclusive licenses, provided they retain meaningful exclusionary rights such as the right to sue.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers may face enforcement actions from patent owners even where an exclusive licensee exists, expanding the number of potential plaintiffs in patent litigation.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting JMOL that Teva's anti-CGRP antibody headache patents were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's grant of JMOL of invalidity for Teva's headache patents, which claim methods of using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies to treat headache. The court found the patent specification's disclosure of prior-art methods of humanization and known anti-CGRP antibodies, combined with disclosed antibody G1, was sufficient to satisfy § 112 requirements. This reversal reinstates a jury verdict of willful infringement against Eli Lilly.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical and biotech patent holders benefit from a more permissive standard for written description and enablement, particularly for genus claims where the specification discloses known methods and at least one working embodiment.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar competitors face broader patent claims surviving validity challenges, potentially extending market exclusivity periods for biologic drugs.

impacts.caseName: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly applied IPR estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) to bar Valve from asserting two invalidity grounds that were not raised in its prior IPR petition.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's application of IPR estoppel, finding insufficient evidence to support estopping one invalidity ground and that the court failed to adequately account for hindsight bias in estopping the other. The decision narrows the scope of IPR estoppel by requiring more rigorous analysis of whether a prior art reference reasonably could have been discovered by a skilled searcher.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in patent litigation retain broader ability to raise invalidity defenses in district court even after IPR proceedings, as courts must carefully evaluate whether prior art was reasonably discoverable before applying estoppel.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face weakened IPR estoppel protections, meaning that surviving IPR does not as effectively foreclose invalidity challenges in subsequent district court litigation.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether there was a legally sufficient evidentiary basis to support the jury's finding that each of the asserted trade secrets was protectable under California law, and whether the related patent-invalidity and counterfeiting claims were properly decided.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of JMOL on trade secret misappropriation claims, holding that the plaintiffs failed to prove that the asserted trade secrets were protectable because the underlying ideas were generally known. The court also reversed on patent invalidity and breach of contract but affirmed the counterfeiting liability finding. The decision vacated the permanent injunction, reasonable royalty, and exemplary damages for trade secrets.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in trade secret cases benefit from heightened scrutiny of whether asserted trade secrets are truly protectable, requiring plaintiffs to demonstrate that information is not generally known in the relevant field.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret holders face greater difficulty sustaining misappropriation claims and obtaining injunctions where the underlying information overlaps with generally known concepts.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the statute of limitations under the Defend Trade Secrets Act had expired before Insulet brought its trade secret misappropriation claim against EOFlow.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury verdict and district court judgment in favor of Insulet, holding that Insulet's DTSA claim was time-barred. The court found that EOFlow was entitled to JMOL because the statute of limitations had expired before suit was filed. The decision vacated the damages award and permanent injunction against EOFlow.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation have a strong defense when the plaintiff had constructive or actual knowledge of the misappropriation well before filing suit, reinforcing the importance of strict limitations compliance.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners risk losing enforcement rights if they delay in filing suit, even when the full scope of misappropriation may not yet be apparent, underscoring the need for prompt legal action upon discovery.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding plaintiff's damages expert testimony and in its calculation of trade secret damages and breach of contract damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court reversed the breach of contract damages ruling and reinstated the jury award. However, it affirmed the denial of Ford's JMOL on trade secret misappropriation liability, sustaining the finding that Ford misappropriated Versata's software trade secrets.
impacts.positiveImplications: Trade secret plaintiffs benefit from expanded consideration of damages methodologies, and the reinstated breach of contract jury award protects software licensors' contractual rights.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop proprietary software during licensing relationships face continued exposure to trade secret misappropriation liability even when they believe they independently developed competing products.

impacts.caseName: Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Pfizer Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the '953 patent could claim priority from a provisional application where a critical substituent range was changed from C2-C12-alkyl to C1-C12-alkyl, and whether Pfizer's intervening public disclosure of nirmatrelvir anticipated the claims.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity, holding that the change from C2 to C1 in the alkyl range was not an obvious typographical error correctable by the court, and thus the patent could not claim priority from its provisional application. Because Pfizer's public disclosure of nirmatrelvir (used in Paxlovid®) occurred before the non-provisional filing date, the claims were anticipated. This decision eliminates Enanta's patent infringement claims against Pfizer's blockbuster COVID-19 treatment.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic and competing pharmaceutical manufacturers benefit from strict enforcement of priority-date requirements, ensuring that errors in provisional applications cannot be retroactively corrected to capture intervening prior art.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face significant risk from even minor drafting errors in provisional applications, as courts may refuse to treat changes as corrections of obvious typographical errors, potentially invalidating entire patent families.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting summary judgment of noninfringement based on extraterritoriality and rejection of VLSI's doctrine of equivalents theory for a patent relating to multi-core processor task selection.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit partially reversed and partially affirmed summary judgment of noninfringement. The court reversed on the extraterritoriality ground, finding genuine disputes of material fact as to where the claimed method was performed, and remanded for further proceedings. The court affirmed the rejection of VLSI's doctrine of equivalents theory on separate grounds.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting claims against semiconductor and technology companies benefit from the court's willingness to find triable issues regarding where method steps occur, preserving infringement claims for domestically directed activities.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies with global manufacturing and testing operations face continued uncertainty about when their overseas activities may constitute domestic patent infringement.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to automated farming data collection, processing, and sharing systems were patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in declining to find the case exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's holding that the asserted claims were patent-ineligible under § 101 as directed to abstract ideas, but vacated and remanded the determination that the case was not exceptional for purposes of attorneys' fees. The court found the claims merely recited conventional data collection and processing steps applied to farming operations without an inventive concept.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies in agriculture and IoT benefit from continued invalidation of broadly drafted data-collection patents, and the remand on exceptionality may support fee-shifting against weak patent assertions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Ag-tech patent holders face heightened difficulty in patenting data-driven farming systems, with additional risk of fee awards if their patent assertions are found exceptional.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in its jury instructions and verdict form on patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101, infringement, and damages for patents directed to wireless building automation systems.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the $11.5 million infringement and damages judgments and remanded for a new trial, finding that the verdict form's single infringement question covering all asserted patents was prejudicially flawed. The court also vacated and remanded for further proceedings on patent eligibility under Alice step two for the '495 patent, while affirming eligibility of other asserted patents and affirming the denial of JMOL on non-infringement.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent defendants benefit from the requirement for patent-specific verdict forms, preventing potential prejudice from bundled infringement questions across multiple patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders risk losing favorable jury verdicts due to procedural flaws in verdict forms and jury instructions, even where underlying infringement evidence may be strong.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming non-uniform constellation designs for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit partially vacated the summary judgment of patent eligibility, finding that some asserted claims required further analysis under Alice, while affirming eligibility for other claims. The court also affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement and damages. The case involves patents incorporated into international broadcasting standards (ATSC 3.0), with significant implications for standard-essential patent licensing.
impacts.positiveImplications: Holders of patents incorporated into industry standards retain strong enforcement positions, with affirmance of infringement and damages determinations supporting robust royalty expectations.
impacts.negativeImplications: Standard-implementers like LG face continued patent infringement exposure for standards-compliant products, and the partial vacatur on eligibility creates ongoing uncertainty for communications patents.

impacts.caseName: Otsuka America Pharmaceutical, Inc. v. Hetero Labs Limited
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly construed the claim terms 'dextromethorphan' and 'quinidine' in a pharmaceutical patent's weight-to-weight ratio limitation, and whether the court permissibly waived the Rule 65(c) bond requirement for a preliminary injunction pending appeal.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the preliminary injunction preventing Hetero from launching a generic competitor to Nuedexta, agreeing with the district court's claim construction. However, the court vacated the waiver of the Rule 65(c) bond requirement, holding that the equitable factors cited were insufficient to justify dispensing with the bond pending appeal. The decision blocks generic entry for the remaining patent term.
impacts.positiveImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies benefit from affirmance of preliminary injunctions blocking generic entry, preserving market exclusivity through patent expiration.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic drug manufacturers face injunctive barriers to market entry, and the bond requirement vacatur means patent holders seeking preliminary injunctions must post security to protect enjoined parties from potential wrongful injunction damages.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify to matters outside personal knowledge for purposes of establishing the on-sale bar under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(b), and whether source code constitutes hearsay.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that Rule 30(b)(6) designees may testify beyond personal knowledge and that computer source code is not hearsay because it consists of machine commands rather than human assertions. The decision validated the use of corporate representative testimony and source code evidence to establish prior art sales.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from broader evidentiary tools to prove invalidity, including corporate designee testimony about historical sales and direct use of source code as non-hearsay evidence.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face expanded evidentiary challenges to their patents' validity, as courts allow corporate representatives to testify about events predating their employment and treat source code as admissible non-hearsay.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Board erred in its obviousness determination of patent claims relating to sensor-based logistics systems, and whether a third-party IPR petition filed on the deadline of the actual defendant raised time-bar issues under 35 U.S.C. § 315(b).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the Board's obviousness determination and remanded for further proceedings, finding errors in the Board's analysis. The court declined to review the challenge to the Board's denial of termination of the IPR. The case highlights concerns about third-party IPR petitions filed in coordination with litigation defendants to circumvent the one-year time bar.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from closer judicial scrutiny of Board obviousness determinations and from the court's willingness to vacate flawed IPR decisions, strengthening patent protection for logistics and supply chain technology.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies using IPR as a defense strategy face uncertainty when third parties file petitions on their behalf, and the remand creates continued litigation costs and patent validity uncertainty.

impacts.caseName: mCom IP, LLC v. City National Bank of Florida
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims surviving IPR can be dismissed on the pleadings as invalid on the same obviousness grounds that invalidated other claims of the same patent, and whether the case qualified as exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed dismissal of a patent infringement complaint for failure to state a claim, finding the surviving claims invalid on the same obviousness grounds that invalidated other claims in IPR. However, the court reversed the § 285 exceptional case fee award and the § 1927 sanction against counsel, finding insufficient grounds to support either determination.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers can obtain early dismissal of infringement claims where surviving patent claims are obviously invalid on the same grounds that invalidated sibling claims in IPR, reducing litigation costs.
impacts.negativeImplications: The reversal of fee and sanction awards limits the deterrent effect against aggressive patent enforcement, as courts must meet higher thresholds to declare cases exceptional or sanction counsel.
